title: Imperfect Women
synopsis: Eleanor was your best friend for twenty years. She's been murdered. You and Mary, the third friend, each know exactly half of the secret that killed her. You have to decide whether to tell each other.

nodes.text: Mary calls at 6:14 a.m. crying. You sit on the edge of the bed and hear the sentence 'Eleanor is dead' and your husband, beside you, does not yet know. The clock keeps moving.

choices.text: Wake your husband
choices.consequence: You commit to “Wake your husband.” The story records the instinct as “Family first” and carries it forward.

choices.text: Get dressed and go to Mary immediately
choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Friend first.

nodes.text: Your husband Robert reacts in a way that is one ratchet off from what you expected. He is sad. He is also, in a way you can't name, alert.

choices.text: Notice the alertness
Ignore it; he loved Eleanor

nodes.text: Mary, at her counter, hands you a coffee with the same chip in the mug she's had since college. She says, before you can speak, 'I knew about Eleanor and someone. I just didn't know who.'

choices.text: Ask her who she suspected
Tell her your half first
choices.consequence: There is no taking “Tell her your half first” back. Trade truths shapes the silence before the next moment arrives.

nodes.text: Eleanor had been having an affair for the last year. You knew because she told you. You don't know with whom. Mary, you suspect, knew the man's name but didn't know it was Eleanor.

choices.text: Tell Mary the affair half now
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Symmetrical truth—follows you into whatever comes next.

choices.text: Wait to see what Mary volunteers

nodes.text: Eleanor had been managing money — yours, Mary's, hers — and you'd noticed a discrepancy two months ago. You'd been planning to ask her about it the day she died. The half-secret is, somehow, becoming whole.

choices.text: Tell Mary about the money
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Honesty—follows you into whatever comes next.

choices.text: Hold the money for now; the affair feels closer to motive
choices.consequence: “Hold the money for now; the affair feels closer to motive” closes one possibility and opens another. The moment leaves a clear note behind: Triage.

nodes.text: Detective Kapoor is kind, careful, slow. She asks you both about Eleanor's life in the past year. She has noticed, you can tell, the small inconsistency between your accounts.

choices.text: Trust her with the affair half
choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Truth.

choices.text: Trust her with the money half
choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Truth.

nodes.text: Eleanor's husband Nathan sits in his kitchen looking smaller than you remember. He says he didn't know about the affair. He says it twice. He looks at you the second time.

choices.text: Believe him
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—He's grieving—follows you into whatever comes next.

choices.text: Watch him more closely

nodes.text: Eleanor's seventeen-year-old, Sophie, asks you, in the back garden, if you knew her mother was unhappy. You realize, again, that 'mother' and 'friend' are different people you each knew.

choices.text: Tell Sophie what you knew
Tell Sophie that her mother loved her

nodes.text: Your husband Robert is, conveniently, out late three nights running. He says it's work. The shoes by the door, when he comes home, are wet. It hasn't rained.

choices.text: Follow Robert one night
Ask Mary if she's noticed the same about her husband
choices.consequence: The choice lands, and the scene changes around it. If it has a name, that name is Compare.

nodes.text: On Eleanor's phone, recovered after a week, is a photo of a hotel-room ceiling. The angle is innocuous to anyone who doesn't know the ceiling. You know the ceiling.

choices.text: Tell Mary you recognize the ceiling
Tell Detective Kapoor

nodes.text: Mary, slowly, admits that her husband Tom has been distant for months. Tom and Robert and Nathan all go to the same gym. The gym is, you realize, three suburbs away from any of their homes.

choices.text: Plan to confront the husbands together
choices.consequence: “Plan to confront the husbands together” closes one possibility and opens another. The moment leaves a clear note behind: United front.

choices.text: Each speak to your own first
choices.consequence: The choice lands, and the scene changes around it. If it has a name, that name is Personal first.

nodes.text: You and Mary corner Robert and Tom in Robert's garage on a Saturday morning. The truth comes out in stages — yes, an affair, no, with one of them, no, neither knew Eleanor would be killed.

choices.text: Believe the parts that exonerate them
Disbelieve until proven

nodes.text: Kapoor calls you in for a quiet meeting. She has, she says, narrowed it. She tells you a name. The name is on neither half of your secret. The room moves.

choices.text: Help her gather what she needs
choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Cooperate fully.

choices.text: Take a breath before responding

nodes.text: An arrest is made. The killer is, almost mundanely, a stranger Eleanor had been planning to leave the marriage for — and who had been planning, in his own ugly way, to leave her too. The motive is small and the loss is enormous.

choices.text: Attend the trial through to verdict
Step back; protect your own family
choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Personal first.

nodes.text: You and Robert sit with a therapist for the first time in your marriage. The truth about his Tuesdays comes out. It is not an affair. It is a less interesting and more painful answer: he has been visiting a sponsor at AA.

choices.text: Apologize fully
Ask why he kept it secret

nodes.text: Mary and you, after, walk every Sunday for a year. You don't talk about Eleanor every walk. You talk about her enough. The friendship that was three is, slowly, two. The two is, sometimes, enough.

choices.text: Make Sundays a permanent ritual
Bring Sophie sometimes

nodes.text: Your own daughter, fifteen, asks you to teach her how to be a friend like you are friends. You sit on the porch and try to think of an answer that isn't a Hallmark card. You tell her, eventually, 'Tell each other things first.'

choices.text: Model that for her with your own friends
choices.consequence: The choice lands, and the scene changes around it. If it has a name, that name is Show.

choices.text: Send her to call her best friend now
choices.consequence: You commit to “Send her to call her best friend now.” The story records the instinct as “Direct” and carries it forward.

nodes.text: Sophie's university acceptance arrives on a Tuesday. You and Mary throw her a party. She gives a small speech and thanks you both. You realize, with a feeling that is both grief and gratitude, that Eleanor is in this room.

choices.text: Tell Sophie about her mother's good qualities
Sit beside Mary and just let it be
choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Presence.

nodes.text: One year after Eleanor died you and Mary and Nathan and Sophie all eat dinner at the same restaurant Eleanor loved. The food is fine. The night is full of stories you'd forgotten. You laugh more than you cry. Eleanor would, you realize, approve.

choices.text: Make this the new tradition
Let it be a one-time thing

nodes.text: Years on, you stop at a photograph of the three of you from a college trip. You realize you don't flinch anymore. You realize you can hold both sadness and gratitude in the same hand. You choose what to do with that hand next.

choices.text: Hand it to Sophie
Keep it on your own wall and call Mary

nodes.text: You and Mary become Sophie's aunts in a real, unofficial way. You attend her graduation. You attend her wedding. At her wedding she names a child after Eleanor. You both cry without performing it.

You and Mary walk for the next thirty years. You bury parents and welcome grandchildren. You speak of Eleanor often, then less often, then often again in the way grief loops. The friendship, in the end, is the answer to the question her death almost asked.
